title: Load Balancing (Basic): Azure Load Balancer
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain why a load balancer is the first step from "one server" to "always open", and what layer 4 means.
- Describe the parts of an Azure Standard Load Balancer: frontend, backend pool, health probe, load-balancing rule, inbound NAT rule and outbound rule.
- Choose between a public and an internal load balancer, and between the distribution modes.
- Explain in plain words how outbound connections and SNAT work, and why new networks need an explicit outbound method.
- Recognise when Application Gateway, Front Door or Traffic Manager is the better tool.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Dewi has done her homework. The storefront now runs on two Ubuntu VMs, vm-web-1 in availability zone 1 and vm-web-2 in zone 2, inside the private subnet Pak Budi designed in Lunch 08. There is just one problem: shoppers know only one address, and right now it points at vm-web-1. If that VM reboots for patching, the shop is closed even though a perfectly good twin is idling in the next zone.

Ibu Sari is direct about it at the Monday meeting. "Two servers are no use if customers can only find one. And Pak Budi says he can't even log in to them now that they have no public addresses." Rizky, the contractor, adds that the servers also fail to download security updates since the network change. Three complaints, one root cause: the servers have no shared front door.

Today's question: how do you give two servers one address, send shoppers only to servers that are healthy, and still let administrators and updates get in and out safely?

Reading

1. One address, many servers: why load balance

A single server is a single point of failure: when it stops, the service stops. In Lunch 02 you met two ways to grow. Scaling up (a bigger VM) has a ceiling and still leaves you with one machine. Scaling out (more VMs) has no such ceiling, but it raises a new question: which server should each customer talk to?

A load balancer answers that question. It owns one address, receives traffic for the whole group, and passes each new connection to one of several servers. It also keeps checking which servers are healthy, so a broken one quietly stops receiving customers. That one component gives Nusantara Retail four things at once:

- Availability. A failed VM, a crashed web service or a whole failed availability zone no longer closes the shop.
- Scale. When the 12.12 sale arrives, Dewi adds a third VM to the group instead of replacing the server.
- Maintenance without downtime. Pak Budi can patch vm-web-1 while vm-web-2 carries the traffic.
- A stable address. Shoppers, DNS records and the payment provider's allow list keep using one IP address while servers come and go behind it.

Load balancers differ in how much of the conversation they understand. Networking people describe this with the layers of the OSI model. You only need two of them:

| Layer 4 (transport) | Layer 7 (application)
What it looks at | IP addresses, ports and protocol (TCP or UDP) | the HTTP request itself: host name, URL path, headers, cookies
What it does with a connection | passes packets straight through to one server | ends the client's connection and opens a new one to the server (a proxy)
Can it route /images to other servers? | no — it never reads the URL | yes
Can it decrypt HTTPS or run a web application firewall? | no | yes
What the server sees as the client | the real client IP address | the proxy's address (client IP in a header)
Azure examples | Azure Load Balancer | Application Gateway, Front Door

Azure Load Balancer is Azure's layer 4 load balancer. It works with any TCP or UDP traffic, not only web traffic, adds very little delay because it never opens or reads your data, and scales to millions of flows. It is a regional service: one load balancer serves resources in one region (a global tier exists too; see section 5). Because it doesn't read requests, it is also the simplest load balancer to reason about, which makes it the right place to start.

Important: Azure Load Balancer comes in Standard and Gateway SKUs. The Basic SKU — and Basic public IP addresses — were retired on September 30, 2025. Older tutorials that use --sku Basic no longer apply. Everything in this course uses Standard, which adds availability zones, secure-by-default networking, outbound rules and a 99.99 % SLA (check the SLA page for its conditions).

2. Anatomy of a Standard load balancer

A load balancer is a small set of named parts that refer to each other. Once you know the parts, the portal wizard, the CLI and a Bicep file all look the same.

Component | What it is | Nusantara Retail example
Frontend IP configuration | the address clients connect to; public (a Standard public IP) or private (an IP from a subnet) | fe-web using the public IP pip-lb-nusa-web
Backend pool | the group of servers that can receive traffic, defined by their NICs or their IP addresses | be-web with the NICs of vm-web-1 and vm-web-2
Health probe | a repeated check of each pool member; only healthy members get new connections | probe-http: HTTP GET /health on port 80 every 5 seconds
Load-balancing rule | maps a frontend IP and port to a backend pool and port, using a probe | rule-http: TCP 80 on the frontend → port 80 on the pool
Inbound NAT rule | forwards one frontend port to one specific VM (port forwarding, not balancing) | nat-ssh-vm1: frontend port 50001 → vm-web-1 port 22
Outbound rule | lets pool members reach the internet through the frontend IP, with ports you allocate | rule-outbound: 10,000 source ports per VM

Public or internal? The frontend decides which kind of load balancer you have:

| Public load balancer | Internal load balancer
Frontend | a Standard public IP address | a private IP address from one of your subnets
Who can reach it | anyone on the internet (filtered by NSGs) | clients inside the virtual network, peered networks and on-premises networks connected by VPN or ExpressRoute
Typical use | the storefront web tier | the order API behind the web tier, a database cluster, firewall appliances
Gives backends internet access? | can, through outbound rules | no; use a NAT gateway or a separate public load balancer

Nusantara Retail will eventually use both: a public load balancer in front of the web servers and an internal one in front of the app subnet from Lunch 08, so the order API is never exposed to the internet.

Two Standard behaviours surprise newcomers. First, a Standard load balancer is secure by default: inbound traffic is blocked until a network security group (NSG) on the subnet or NIC allows it. The NSG sees the shopper's real IP address, because a layer 4 load balancer does not replace the source address. Second, the backend pool can be defined by NIC or by IP address. Pools built from NICs are the recommended choice for virtual machines and give the most predictable outbound behaviour.

3. Health probes and how traffic is shared

A load balancer is only as smart as its health probe. Every few seconds the platform sends a probe to every pool member and records the answer. Standard load balancers support three probe types:

Probe type | Healthy when… | Good for
TCP | the server completes the TCP handshake on the port | any TCP service; it proves only that something is listening
HTTP | an HTTP GET on your path returns 200 OK | web servers; let the application decide whether it is healthy
HTTPS | like HTTP, but over TLS | web servers that only listen on HTTPS (no client certificates)

Some details are worth remembering:

- Probes come from 168.63.129.16. In NSG rules this source is represented by the AzureLoadBalancer service tag. A default NSG rule allows it, but a home-made "deny everything" rule with a higher priority silently blocks the probes, and then every server looks dead.
- The interval is configurable, with a minimum of 5 seconds. The portal suggests 5 seconds; the CLI and templates default to 15. For HTTP probes, any answer other than 200 marks the server down immediately; a probe that gets no reply at all times out after 30 seconds at most.
- A failed probe affects new connections only. Shoppers already connected to the failing server keep their TCP connection until it closes or times out; new connections go to healthy members. If every member is down, a Standard load balancer sends no new connections anywhere.
- Probe something meaningful. A TCP probe on port 80 stays green when the web application returns errors. An HTTP probe on a /health page that the application controls can say "take me out of rotation" before maintenance.

Tip: Give every application a cheap /health page and probe it over HTTP. Make it check what the server itself needs (disk space, its own configuration), but be careful about checking shared dependencies: if /health fails whenever the shared database is slow, every server fails at once and the load balancer has nowhere to send anyone.

How does the load balancer choose a server for each new connection? By default it computes a hash of five values — the 5-tuple: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and protocol. The same connection always hashes to the same server, so packets of one conversation stay together. A new connection from the same browser uses a new source port, so it can land on the other server. Across thousands of shoppers this spreads load evenly; with only a handful of clients behind one company proxy, the spread can be lopsided.

Distribution mode | Hash of | Behaviour | Use it when
None (default, hash-based) | 5-tuple | each new connection may go to any healthy server | the application keeps no session data on the server
Client IP | source IP + destination IP | one client IP keeps going to the same server | a legacy app stores the shopping cart in server memory
Client IP and protocol | source IP + destination IP + protocol | the same, per protocol | an app opens related TCP and UDP sessions that must meet on one server

Session persistence (the two "Client IP" modes) is a crutch, not a design. If a server fails, its sessions are lost anyway; many shoppers behind one mobile carrier or office proxy look like a single client IP; and adding a server reshuffles everybody. The durable fix is to keep session state outside the VMs, for example in a database or cache.

Two more rule settings matter in practice. The idle timeout (4 minutes by default) closes TCP connections that send nothing; you can raise it within limits, and you should enable TCP reset so both ends hear about the closure instead of discovering it later. HA ports, another rule setting, appear in section 5.

4. Getting in and getting out: inbound NAT rules, outbound rules and SNAT

Getting in to one server. Load-balancing rules spread traffic, but an administrator who wants to SSH to vm-web-1 needs to reach that VM. An inbound NAT rule forwards one frontend port to one VM's port: connect to the frontend IP on port 50001 and you arrive at vm-web-1 on port 22. The NSG evaluates the translated packet, so it must allow port 22, ideally from a single admin address. A newer form of the rule targets a whole backend pool with a port range and assigns each member its own frontend port; the older pool-based inbound NAT pools used by scale sets retire on September 30, 2027. For day-to-day administration, Azure Bastion (Lunch 06) is the safer habit — no management port is exposed to the internet at all.

Getting out. Servers also start conversations: downloading updates, calling the payment provider, sending e-mail through a mail service. In Lunch 08 you learned that virtual networks created with API versions released after March 31, 2026 get private subnets by default, so VMs have no implicit internet access, and that a Standard load balancer adds none by itself. Something must provide outbound access explicitly.

That something uses SNAT — source network address translation. Think of the head office switchboard. Two hundred employees share one public phone number. When an employee calls out, the operator notes which line the call used, so that when the other party answers, the call is put through to the right desk. The public number is the frontend IP; each "line" is a SNAT port. One public IP offers about 64,000 of them for outbound connections, shared by all the VMs that use it.

Each simultaneous connection to the same destination IP and port needs its own SNAT port. A server that opens thousands of short connections to one API, without reusing them, can run out of its share — SNAT port exhaustion — and new outbound calls fail while the rest of the VM looks fine.

An outbound rule is how you take control. You choose which frontend IPs to use, which backend pool may leave, the protocols, an idle timeout (4–120 minutes) and, most importantly, how many SNAT ports each VM gets, in multiples of 8. Two VMs could receive up to 32,000 ports each from one IP; adding frontend IPs adds ports. Without an outbound rule, a load-balancing rule can still provide outbound access implicitly, but with a small default allocation (at most 1,024 ports per VM, fewer in large pools). Microsoft recommends against relying on that.

The options for outbound access, best first:

Method | Notes
NAT gateway on the subnet | the recommended choice: dynamic port allocation, scales well, takes precedence over the others
Public IP on the VM | fine for a single special server; every VM gets its own exposed address
Load balancer outbound rules | good when the VMs already sit behind a public load balancer; you size the ports
Load-balancing rule without outbound rules | implicit, small fixed allocation — avoid for production
Default outbound access | implicit and changing; not available in private subnets — avoid

Warning: When you add an outbound rule that uses the same frontend IP as a load-balancing rule, the rule must have outbound SNAT disabled (--disable-outbound-snat true), otherwise creating the outbound rule fails. The reverse mistake hurts more: disable SNAT on the rule but forget the outbound rule, and the VMs lose internet access — updates and payment calls fail while the website itself looks healthy.

5. Zones and special flavours: HA ports, gateway and global load balancers

Zones. In Lunch 03 you met zone-redundant and zonal resources. A load balancer frontend can be either. A zone-redundant frontend is served from all zones of the region, so it survives the loss of any one of them; a zonal frontend is pinned to one zone and fails with it. Standard public IPs created with zones 1, 2 and 3 are zone-redundant, and Microsoft now treats Standard public IPs created without a zone as zone-redundant in regions that have zones. Spread the backend VMs across zones too, as Dewi did. A frontend that survives a zone failure does not help if both servers sat in that zone.

HA ports. On an internal Standard load balancer, a rule with protocol All and port 0 balances every TCP and UDP flow on every port. That is how firewall appliances in a hub network are made highly available (Lunch 25): one rule, all traffic, and a probe that reflects the health of the whole appliance.

Gateway Load Balancer. A separate SKU for inserting third-party network virtual appliances — firewalls, intrusion detection, packet analysers — transparently into the path. You chain it to a public load balancer frontend or a VM's public IP, and traffic visits the appliances before reaching your application, with no route tables to maintain.

Global (cross-region) load balancer. A Standard load balancer can also be created in the global tier. It offers one static anycast public IP that is advertised from many Azure regions, and its backend pool contains regional public load balancers. Shoppers enter Microsoft's network at the nearest participating region and are sent to the closest healthy regional deployment; if a region fails, traffic moves within seconds because no DNS caching is involved. It is still layer 4, supports public frontends only, and must be created in one of a list of home regions (Southeast Asia and East Asia are on it; check the documentation for others). Lunch 27 compares it with the global layer 7 options.

6. Choosing your load balancer — and Nusantara's new front door

Azure has four main load balancing services, and choosing between them is a favourite exam and interview topic. Two questions do most of the work: is it web traffic that needs layer 7 features? and is it regional or global?

| Azure Load Balancer | Application Gateway | Azure Front Door | Traffic Manager
Layer | 4 (TCP/UDP) | 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) | 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) | DNS
Scope | regional (global tier for cross-region) | regional | global, at Microsoft's edge | global
Sees your traffic? | passes it through | yes, as a proxy in your network | yes, as a proxy at the edge | no — it only answers DNS queries
Signature features | any protocol, very low latency, outbound rules, HA ports | path and host routing, TLS termination, WAF, autoscale | caching, fast global failover, WAF, edge TLS | priority, weighted, performance and geographic routing
Nusantara Retail example | today's web VMs; the internal order API | /images/* to an images app, with a WAF | shoppers from Medan to Makassar | DNS failover between two regions

This lunch builds the first column. Lunch 27 covers the other three in depth, including how they combine — Front Door in front of Application Gateway, for example.

Here is Nusantara Retail's design after today. A Standard public load balancer, lb-nusa-web, owns a zone-redundant frontend IP. Its backend pool holds the NICs of vm-web-1 (zone 1) and vm-web-2 (zone 2). An HTTP probe asks each server for /health every 5 seconds, and a rule sends TCP 80 to healthy servers only. An inbound NAT rule gives Pak Budi emergency SSH to vm-web-1 from the office IP until Bastion arrives, and an outbound rule lets both servers reach the update mirrors and the payment provider through the same public IP — which the payment provider can put on its allow list. The answer to Ibu Sari's question has changed: if one server dies, shoppers notice nothing beyond a retried page; if a zone fails, the shop stays open; if the whole region fails, that is a story for Lunches 17 and 27.

For production, the same design would run in Indonesia Central (Jakarta), which has three availability zones and keeps customer data in Indonesia. The labs use Southeast Asia for the widest service availability; the design is identical.

Pause and think: Nusantara Retail's payment provider allows calls only from known IP addresses. Which address will the provider see when vm-web-2 calls it today — and what would change if Dewi replaced the outbound rule with a NAT gateway that has its own public IP?

Advanced partner: Lunch 27 · Load Balancing (Advanced) (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/lunches/27-load-balancing-advanced.html) covers Application Gateway, Front Door and Traffic Manager.

Field notes from Stefanus

A failover you have never tested is only a hope. In design reviews I ask one question about every load-balanced service: when did you last stop one of these servers on purpose? If the answer is "never", I don't call it highly available yet. Before go-live I stop the web service on each backend in turn, in working hours, while the team watches: the probe should take it out within seconds and the shop should keep answering. Then I test the way out, because it fails quietly: from inside each VM I call the payment API or the update mirror and check which public address the other side sees. And when every backend turns unhealthy at once, I check the probe and the NSG before I touch a server.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Azure Load Balancer health probes (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/load-balancer/load-balancer-custom-probe-overview) — probe types, intervals and what happens to connections when probes fail.
- Microsoft Learn: Source Network Address Translation (SNAT) for outbound connections (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/load-balancer/load-balancer-outbound-connections) — the outbound options ranked, SNAT ports and how to avoid exhaustion.
- Microsoft Learn: Azure Load Balancer SKUs (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/load-balancer/skus) — what Standard offers and the Basic retirement notice.
- Azure Architecture Center: Load balancing options (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/architecture/guide/technology-choices/load-balancing-overview) — the official guide to choosing between Azure's load balancers; a preview of Lunch 27.

quiz.q: Dewi's old storefront code keeps each shopping cart in the web server's memory. Since the load balancer went live, some customers lose their cart halfway through checkout. What can you change on the load balancer today, and what is the better long-term fix?
quiz.a: Switch the rule to Client IP session persistence; long term, keep session state outside the VMs (a database or cache). Why: the default 5-tuple hash can send each new connection to a different server.

quiz.q: Rizky adds a rule Deny-All-Inbound (priority 200) to nsg-web to "tighten security". The rule Allow-HTTP-Internet (priority 100) is still there, yet within seconds the storefront stops answering through the load balancer. Both VMs serve pages locally. What happened?
quiz.a: The deny rule blocks the health probes from 168.63.129.16 (service tag AzureLoadBalancer), so every member is marked down. Allow AzureLoadBalancer with a priority number below 200. Why: the default probe allow rule has priority 65001 and loses to any custom deny.

quiz.q: Pak Budi creates an inbound NAT rule from frontend port 50001 to vm-web-1 port 22 and an NSG rule allowing TCP 50001 from his office IP. SSH still times out. What is wrong?
quiz.a: The NSG must allow destination port 22. Why: the NSG evaluates the packet after the load balancer has translated the port.

quiz.q: After a network redesign the web servers sit in a private subnet behind the load balancer, and the rule has outbound SNAT disabled. Security updates now fail. Give two ways to fix it.
quiz.a: Add an outbound rule for the backend pool, or attach a NAT gateway to the subnet (recommended). Why: private subnets have no default outbound access, and a Standard load balancer gives none unless you configure it.

quiz.q: Nusantara Retail wants shop.nusantararetail.co.id/images/* served by a separate pool of image servers and wants a web application firewall in front of everything. Is Azure Load Balancer the right tool?
quiz.a: No — use Application Gateway (regional) or Azure Front Door (global), covered in Lunch 27. Why: a layer 4 load balancer never reads the URL path, so it can neither route by path nor inspect requests.

takeaways: A load balancer gives a group of servers one address and sends new connections only to healthy members; Azure Load Balancer does it at layer 4, for any TCP or UDP traffic.
Use the Standard SKU (Basic retired on September 30, 2025). It is secure by default: NSGs must allow client traffic and the AzureLoadBalancer probes.
The parts are always the same: frontend IP, backend pool, health probe, load-balancing rule, plus inbound NAT rules to reach one VM and outbound rules to let the pool out.
The 5-tuple hash spreads connections; session persistence pins a client IP to a server but doesn't replace keeping state off the VMs.
Outbound access must be explicit: size SNAT ports with outbound rules or prefer a NAT gateway. A zone-redundant frontend plus VMs in several zones survives a zone failure.

lab.title: Keep the shop open when a server fails
lab.text:
What you'll build

Nusantara Retail's storefront now runs on two small web servers, one in availability zone 1 and one in zone 2. Neither has a public IP address, and they sit in a private subnet with no default internet access. You give them one front door: a Standard public load balancer with a zone-redundant frontend IP, a health probe that checks /health, and a rule that spreads shoppers across both servers. Then you break one server on purpose and watch the shop stay open, add an inbound NAT rule so an administrator can still reach vm-web-1 over SSH, and add an outbound rule so the servers can reach the internet for updates and the payment provider.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)).
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- About 4 vCPUs of free quota in your region (two Standard_B2ats_v2 VMs with 2 vCPUs each). bash ../common/check-environment.sh shows it.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/09-load-balancing-basic
source ../common/config.sh
source lab.env          # the resource names this lab uses: RG, LB, PIP, POOL, PROBE, ...
RG=$(rg_name 09)

- Create the starting point — takes about 6–10 minutes (two VMs, then a quick check that each web server answers):

bash setup.sh

While you wait, reread section 3 of the lunch (health probes). The script creates nsg-web (allows TCP 80 from the Internet and AzureLoadBalancer service tags), the virtual network vnet-nusa-web with the private subnet snet-web, and vm-web-1/vm-web-2 running the course's tiny web server (/ shows the VM name and zone, /health answers ok).

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist (two VMs, a load balancer and a public IP). Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway. If Cloud Shell times out, reconnect and rerun the cd and both source lines above before you continue.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–7 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | run bash setup.sh, read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Look at the starting point

Before adding a load balancer, confirm what you are balancing: two servers in two zones, no public IPs, and a subnet that cannot reach the internet on its own.

az vm list -g "$RG" -d \
  --query "[].{name:name, zone:zones[0], privateIp:privateIps, publicIp:publicIps}" -o table

az network vnet subnet show -g "$RG" --vnet-name "$VNET" -n "$SUBNET" \
  --query "{prefix:addressPrefix, defaultOutboundAccess:defaultOutboundAccess, nsg:networkSecurityGroup.id}" -o yaml

az network nsg rule list -g "$RG" --nsg-name "$NSG" \
  --query "[].{name:name, priority:priority, source:sourceAddressPrefix, port:destinationPortRange}" -o table

# Ask vm-web-1 for its own home page (Run Command works without any public IP)
az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM1" --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "curl -s localhost | grep 'Served by'" --query "value[0].message" -o tsv

Checkpoint: two VMs in zones 1 and 2 with private IPs 10.9.1.x and an empty public IP column; defaultOutboundAccess: false; two NSG rules for port 80; and the page from vm-web-1 says Served by vm-web-1 in availability zone 1.

Task 2 · Create a zone-redundant frontend IP

Shoppers need one stable address. A Standard public IP spread across zones 1, 2 and 3 keeps answering even if a whole zone fails. (Basic public IPs were retired on September 30, 2025.)

az network public-ip create -g "$RG" -n "$PIP" -l "$LOCATION" \
  --sku Standard --allocation-method Static --zone 1 2 3 --output none

az network public-ip show -g "$RG" -n "$PIP" \
  --query "{sku:sku.name, zones:join(',', zones), address:ipAddress}" -o table

Checkpoint: Standard, zones 1,2,3, and an IP address. lb_ip (a helper from lab.env) prints the same address.

Task 3 · Create the load balancer and fill the backend pool

Create a Standard load balancer that uses the IP as its frontend, with an empty backend pool. Then put both servers' network interfaces into the pool. Adding NICs (rather than IP addresses) is the recommended pool type.

az network lb create -g "$RG" -n "$LB" -l "$LOCATION" --sku Standard \
  --public-ip-address "$PIP" --frontend-ip-name "$FE" --backend-pool-name "$POOL" --output none

for nic in "$NIC1" "$NIC2"; do
  az network nic ip-config address-pool add -g "$RG" --nic-name "$nic" \
    --ip-config-name "$IPCONFIG" --lb-name "$LB" --address-pool "$POOL" --output none
done

az network lb address-pool show -g "$RG" --lb-name "$LB" -n "$POOL" \
  --query "backendIPConfigurations[].id" -o tsv

Now try the frontend: curl -s --max-time 5 "http://$(lb_ip)/" || echo "no answer". Nothing answers yet — a load balancer forwards nothing until a rule tells it which traffic to send where.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Load balancers › Create: SKU Standard, Type Public, Tier Regional; on Frontend IP configuration choose the existing pip-lb-nusa-web; on Backend pools add vm-web-1 and vm-web-2 (configuration type NIC). Skip rules for now, review, create — then come back for Task 4. The portal wizard shows every component of section 2 of the lunch on one screen.

Checkpoint: two IDs ending in nic-vm-web-1/ipConfigurations/ipconfig1 and nic-vm-web-2/ipConfigurations/ipconfig1.

Task 4 · Add a health probe and a load-balancing rule

The probe asks every pool member for /health every 5 seconds; only members that answer 200 OK receive new connections. The rule says: TCP traffic arriving on frontend port 80 goes to port 80 on healthy pool members.

az network lb probe create -g "$RG" --lb-name "$LB" -n "$PROBE" \
  --protocol Http --port 80 --path /health --interval 5 --output none

az network lb rule create -g "$RG" --lb-name "$LB" -n "$RULE" \
  --protocol Tcp --frontend-port 80 --backend-port 80 \
  --frontend-ip "$FE" --backend-pool-name "$POOL" --probe "$PROBE" \
  --disable-outbound-snat true --idle-timeout 15 --enable-tcp-reset true --output none

What the flags mean:

- --interval 5 — probe every 5 seconds. The CLI default is 15 seconds; the portal suggests 5.
- --disable-outbound-snat true — this rule handles inbound traffic only. You give the servers outbound access deliberately in Task 7, with an outbound rule.
- --idle-timeout 15 --enable-tcp-reset true — idle connections are closed after 15 minutes, and both ends are told with a TCP reset instead of being silently dropped.

Wait about 30 seconds for the first probes, then send ten requests and see who answers:

who_answers 10
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" "http://$(lb_ip)/"

Checkpoint: the lines mention both vm-web-1 … zone 1 and vm-web-2 … zone 2 (not strictly alternating — each new connection is placed by a hash), and the status is HTTP 200. Open http://<frontend IP> in your browser and refresh a few times.

Task 5 · Fail a server and watch the shop stay open

Stop the web service on vm-web-2 — the VM keeps running, but nothing answers on port 80 any more, just like a crashed application.

az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM2" --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "systemctl stop nusa-web && echo stopped" --query "value[0].message" -o tsv

who_answers 10

Within a few seconds of the service stopping, the probe to vm-web-2 fails and every new connection goes to vm-web-1. The shop stays open; shoppers do not need a new address. Now repair the server:

az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM2" --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "systemctl start nusa-web && echo started" --query "value[0].message" -o tsv

who_answers 10

Tip: Prefer the portal? Open lb-nusa-web › Monitoring › Metrics, choose the metric Health Probe Status and Apply splitting by Backend IP Address. Stop and start the service again and watch one line drop to 0 % and recover (metrics arrive with a delay of a minute or two).

Checkpoint: while the service is stopped, every answer says vm-web-1; after you start it again, vm-web-2 reappears without you touching the load balancer.

Task 6 · Reach one VM with an inbound NAT rule

The servers have no public IPs, but an administrator sometimes needs SSH. An inbound NAT rule forwards one frontend port to one VM: here 50001 on the frontend goes to port 22 on vm-web-1. It is port forwarding, not load balancing — it always lands on the same VM.

az network lb inbound-nat-rule create -g "$RG" --lb-name "$LB" -n "$NAT_RULE" \
  --protocol Tcp --frontend-ip "$FE" --frontend-port "$NAT_PORT" --backend-port 22 --output none

az network nic ip-config inbound-nat-rule add -g "$RG" --nic-name "$NIC1" \
  --ip-config-name "$IPCONFIG" --lb-name "$LB" --inbound-nat-rule "$NAT_RULE" --output none

The load balancer is secure by default, so the NSG must also allow the traffic. The NSG evaluates the packet after translation, so the rule opens port 22 (not 50001) — and only for your own address:

MY_IP=$(my_public_ip); echo "Your public IP: $MY_IP"

az network nsg rule create -g "$RG" --nsg-name "$NSG" -n Allow-SSH-MyIP \
  --priority 120 --direction Inbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp \
  --source-address-prefixes "${MY_IP}/32" --source-port-ranges '*' \
  --destination-address-prefixes '*' --destination-port-ranges 22 --output none

ssh -p "$NAT_PORT" -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new "${ADMIN_USER}@$(lb_ip)" 'hostname; cat /var/www/nusa/health'

setup.sh created the VMs with --generate-ssh-keys, so the key pair is in ~/.ssh of this Cloud Shell.

Checkpoint: the SSH command prints vm-web-1 and ok. Run it three times — it is always vm-web-1. In production you would prefer Azure Bastion (Lunch 06) over opening SSH through a public frontend.

Task 7 · Give the backends a way out with an outbound rule

The subnet is private and the load-balancing rule has outbound SNAT disabled, so the servers cannot reach the internet — no updates, no calls to the payment provider. Prove it first:

az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM1" --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "curl -s --max-time 10 https://api.ipify.org || echo no-outbound" \
  --query "value[0].message" -o tsv

You should see no-outbound. Now add an outbound rule: the servers in be-web leave through the frontend IP, and each VM gets 10,000 SNAT ports (a multiple of 8; two VMs × 10,000 fits easily in the 64,000 ports one public IP offers).

az network lb outbound-rule create -g "$RG" --lb-name "$LB" -n "$OUT_RULE" \
  --frontend-ip-configs "$FE" --address-pool "$POOL" --protocol All \
  --outbound-ports 10000 --idle-timeout 15 --enable-tcp-reset true --output none

Run the same Run Command test again (give it a minute), and compare the answer with lb_ip.

Checkpoint: vm-web-1 now reaches api.ipify.org, and the address the internet sees is your frontend IP. For many VMs or heavy outbound traffic, a NAT gateway on the subnet is the more scalable choice (Lunch 08).

Break it and fix it

Change the probe path to a page that does not exist (a one-letter typo):

az network lb probe update -g "$RG" --lb-name "$LB" -n "$PROBE" --path /healthz --output none
sleep 20
who_answers 5

Symptom: every request says (no answer) — yet both VMs are running and their web servers are fine.

Hint

Ask each server what the probe asks for: az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM1" --command-id RunShellScript --scripts "curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' localhost/healthz" returns 404. An HTTP probe treats anything except 200 as "down". With all members down, a Standard load balancer sends no new connections anywhere.

Fix

az network lb probe update -g "$RG" --lb-name "$LB" -n "$PROBE" --path /health --output none
sleep 20
who_answers 5

Lesson: when everything behind a load balancer "fails" at once, check the probe before you check the servers.

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. The last check runs a command on vm-web-1 and takes about 30 seconds.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
who_answers prints (no answer) for every request | probe failing (wrong path or port), NSG blocking port 80, or no rule yet | az network lb probe show -g "$RG" --lb-name "$LB" -n "$PROBE" -o table; check nsg-web rules; confirm rule-http exists
Only one VM ever answers | the other VM is not in the pool, or its web service is stopped | az network lb address-pool show ... --query "backendIPConfigurations[].id"; run systemctl start nusa-web on it with Run Command
setup.sh reports no answer from /health yet | cloud-init is still running on a slow first boot | wait two minutes, then: az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM1" --command-id RunShellScript --scripts "curl -s localhost/health"
az vm create fails with SkuNotAvailable | the VM size is not offered in that zone or region | export VM_SIZE_SMALL=Standard_B2ts_v2, run source ../common/config.sh again, rerun bash setup.sh
az vm create fails with OperationNotAllowed mentioning quota | not enough regional vCPU quota | delete VMs from other labs, or use another region (export LOCATION=..., then source ../common/config.sh again)
Outbound rule fails with LoadBalancingRuleMustDisableSNATSinceSameFrontendIPConfigurationIsReferencedByOutboundRule | the load-balancing rule still does automatic outbound SNAT on the same frontend | az network lb rule update -g "$RG" --lb-name "$LB" -n "$RULE" --disable-outbound-snat true
ssh: connect to host … port 50001: Connection timed out | NSG has no allow for port 22 from your IP, NAT rule not attached to the NIC, or Cloud Shell's public IP changed | rerun MY_IP=$(my_public_ip) and the NSG rule command; check az network nic show -g "$RG" -n "$NIC1" --query "ipConfigurations[0].loadBalancerInboundNatRules"
Permission denied (publickey) | you are not in the Cloud Shell where setup.sh generated the key | az vm user update -g "$RG" -n "$VM1" -u "$ADMIN_USER" --ssh-key-value ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub
Run Command says another operation is in progress | one Run Command at a time per VM | wait a minute and run it again

Challenge brief

Run bash setup.sh, then build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep), using the names from lab.env:

1. A Standard public load balancer lb-nusa-web whose frontend uses a zone-redundant Standard public IP.
2. A NIC-based backend pool be-web that contains the NICs of vm-web-1 and vm-web-2.
3. An HTTP health probe probe-http on port 80, path /health.
4. A load-balancing rule rule-http: TCP 80 → 80, using probe-http, with outbound SNAT disabled on the rule.
5. An inbound NAT rule nat-ssh-vm1: frontend port 50001 → port 22 on vm-web-1 (SSH allowed only from your IP).
6. An outbound rule rule-outbound that gives the backend pool internet access through the frontend IP.
7. Both servers answer http://<frontend IP>/ with HTTP 200.

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode.
